    // climate & people · history of science
    Pioneer Women in Climate
    For years I have been documenting the women who built the foundations of meteorology and climate science, and whose contributions were overlooked, delayed, or attributed to others. This is an ongoing research project, and it is still growing.
    Text extracted and adapted from the Preface of my PhD dissertation (2020) and from a peer-reviewed article in Tiempo y Clima (2025).
  

  

    
      FILE Nº 001
      
        E.N.F
        
          EUNICE NEWTON FOOTE
          1819 – 1888 · United States
          Physicist · Pioneered greenhouse effect research
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        In 1856, Foote demonstrated that CO₂ traps heat more than any other gas — the first experimental evidence of the greenhouse effect. Because she was a woman, she was not allowed to present her own work at the AAAS meeting. A man read it on her behalf.
        Three years later, John Tyndall published similar results and received full credit. Newton Foote's work went unrecognised for over 150 years. Today, average CO₂ levels are above 420 ppm. She predicted this would warm the Earth. She was right.
        She also participated in the Seneca Falls Convention, fighting for women's rights. Her paper "Circumstances Affecting the Heat of the Sun's Rays" was never formally published.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 002
      
        F.M.B
        
          FELISA MARTÍN BRAVO
          1898 – 1979 · Spain
          Meteorologist · First woman at AEMET
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        First woman to earn a PhD in physics in Spain. In 1931 she passed the national exams to enter AEMET, becoming the first Spanish female meteorologist, and the only one until 1935.
        She collaborated with Nobel Prize winner Charles Thomson Rees Wilson at Cambridge. The Spanish Civil War halted her career, as it did for so many women scientists. Unlike most, she was allowed to return to AEMET under the dictatorship.
        Between 1937 and 1940 she directed the Igeldo Meteorological Observatory. Between 1973 and 1974 she served as president of the Spanish Association of Meteorology — another first.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 003
      
        J.E.L
        
          JEAN ELIZABETH LABY
          1915 – 2008 · Australia
          Physicist · Atmospheric aerosols & stratosphere
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        WWII redirected her path: instead of joining the Bureau of Meteorology as planned, she was assigned to produce optical instruments for the armed forces.
        She worked at the University of Melbourne for over forty years. In 1959, she became the first woman to obtain a PhD in Physics in Australia. Her research covered cosmic rays, atmospheric aerosols, ozone and water vapour in the stratosphere.
        In 2009, one year after her death, she was inducted into the Victorian Honour Roll of Women.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 004
      
        A.M
        
          ANNA MANI
          1918 – 2001 · India
          Meteorologist · Ozone & weather instruments
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        Despite years of research on spectroscopy and a completed dissertation, Madras University denied her a PhD because she lacked a master's degree. Undeterred, she obtained a scholarship to Imperial College London.
        She made India self-sufficient in weather instruments — before her work, all instruments were imported from England. She pioneered ozone research in India long before the scientific community understood its importance.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 005
      
        E.E.F
        
          EDITH ELIZABETH FARKAS
          1921 – 2000 · Hungary / New Zealand
          Meteorologist · Ozone monitoring · Antarctica
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        Fled Hungary during WWII, eventually emigrating to New Zealand as a refugee in 1949. Her university qualifications were not recognised, forcing her to start over in a language she had never formally studied.
        She earned a Master's degree and in 1951 joined MetService, where she worked for over 35 years conducting world-leading ozone monitoring research.
        In 1975, she became the first woman from MetService — and one of the first women ever — to set foot in Antarctica.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 006
      
        J.S
        
          JOANNE SIMPSON
          1923 – 2010 · United States
          Meteorologist · First woman PhD in meteorology (US)
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        "Clouds are a good subject for a little girl to study." — Carl Gustav Rossby, predicting Simpson would never find a job as a meteorologist if she got her PhD.
        In 1949 she proved him wrong, becoming the first woman in the United States to hold a PhD in Meteorology. She developed the first cloud model and co-proposed the Hot Towers hypothesis of tropical convection.
        She authored over 190 peer-reviewed articles and became Chief Scientist for Meteorology at NASA. In 2002 she received the International Meteorological Organization Prize — the first woman ever to do so.
      
    

    
      FILE Nº 007
      
        J.B.B
        
          JUNE BACON-BERCEY
          1928 – 2019 · United States
          Meteorologist · First African-American woman in TV weather
          ▼ open file
        
      
      
        First African-American woman to earn a degree in atmospheric sciences in the US (UCLA, 1954) and one of the first to deliver weather on television. "I didn't want to be seen as just a pretty face."
        She became chief meteorologist and in 1972 received the AMS Seal of Approval — the first woman and first African-American to do so.
        In 1977 she won a TV game show and used part of her winnings to create an AGU scholarship for women studying atmospheric sciences. A legacy that outlasted her career.

  Weather Station Coverage across Spain

  
    
  

  
    ↓ download map
  

  
    Choropleth map showing the distance from each Spanish municipality to the nearest Spanish Met Service (AEMET) weather station. Areas in deep blue represent distances higher than 15 km from the closest station, revealing significant coverage gaps across the territory.

    The information behind this map is the gaps in Spain's weather-observation network, particularly in rural and mountainous areas, where investment in climate infrastructure has historically been low. Those gaps are not merely cartographic — they have real consequences.

    
      The lack of weather station coverage limits the ability to detect and anticipate extreme events such as heatwaves, heavy rainfall, and storms. Without observations, there is no data assimilation. Without data assimilation, forecast models are blind in precisely the areas that matter most during high-impact events.
    

    In the context of climate change, this is not a minor technical detail. Extreme precipitation events, prolonged droughts, and heat episodes are becoming more frequent and more intense across the Iberian Peninsula. Some of the ability to monitor those events depends on whether there is a ground station.

    
      
        
        Original LinkedIn post
      
    

    



Tools
Python · GeoPandas · Matplotlib


Context
#30DayMapChallenge 2025 · Day 7: Accessibility


Data
AEMET OpenData · Administrative boundaries CNIG-IGN




  

  
    How it was made · selected code

    1 · Fetch station data from AEMET OpenData API
    url = "https://opendata.aemet.es/opendata/api/observacion/convencional/todas"
response = requests.get(url, headers={"api_key": API_KEY})
data_url = response.json()["datos"]

observaciones = requests.get(data_url).json()
df = pd.DataFrame(observaciones)

    2 · Compute distance from each municipality to nearest station
    # Reproject to metric CRS for accurate distance calculation
municipios_m = municipios.to_crs(3035)
stations_m   = gdf_stations.to_crs(3035)

municipios_dist = municipios_m.sjoin_nearest(
    stations_m[["geometry"]],
    how="left",
    distance_col="nearest_dist_m")
municipios_dist["nearest_dist_km"] = municipios_dist["nearest_dist_m"] / 1000.0

    3 · Plot choropleth map
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 10))

municipios_dist.plot(
    ax=ax,
    column="nearest_dist_km",
    cmap=cmap,
    norm=norm,
    linewidth=0.1,
    edgecolor="white")

gdf_stations.plot(ax=ax, color="orange", marker="^",
                  markersize=8, alpha=0.6, label="AEMET stations")

ax.set_title("Areas with Fewer Nearby Spanish Met Service Weather Stations",
    fontsize=11, color="dimgray", pad=10)
ax.set_axis_off()

  CO₂ and Sea Ice Extent

  
    
      
    
  

  
    ↓ download animation
  

  
    Each frame in this animation is a pair of 3D bubbles growing and shrinking through time to make two opposing trends visible. The red bubble tracks atmospheric CO₂ concentration measured at Mauna Loa: it grows relentlessly, decade after decade. The blue bubble tracks Arctic sea ice extent from the Copernicus Marine Service: it shrinks over time.

    The choice of bubbles was deliberate. A line chart can show the same data, but there is something about volume — about watching one thing expand while another collapses — that communicates the imbalance more viscerally. Climate change is not a subtle trend. The visual language should reflect that.

    
      CO₂ has risen from around 315 ppm in the late 1950s to over 420 ppm today. Over the same period, Arctic sea ice has lost roughly 13% of its extent per decade. These are not independent signals — they are two sides of the same story.
    

    
      
        
        Original LinkedIn post
      
    

    



Tools
Python · Matplotlib · FuncAnimation · PyVista


Context
Climate communication · Personal project


Data
NOAA (Mauna Loa CO₂) · Copernicus Marine Service (sea ice extent)




  

  
    How it was made · PyVista code

    1 · Load data: CO₂ from NOAA, sea ice from Copernicus
    url_co2 = "https://gml.noaa.gov/webdata/ccgg/trends/co2/co2_annmean_mlo.csv"
df_co2 = pd.read_csv(url_co2, comment="#", header=None,
                     names=["year", "CO2_ppm", "unc"])
df_co2["year"] = df_co2["year"].astype(int)

seaice = pd.read_csv("ARCTIC_OMI_SI_extent_obs_annual.csv")
seaice = seaice.rename(columns={"extent_million_km2": "SeaIce_million_km2"})

data = pd.merge(df_co2, seaice, on="year", how="inner")
data = data[(data["year"] >= 1979) & (data["year"] <= 2023)]

    2 · Scale bubble sizes and set up the PyVista scene
    import pyvista as pv

scale_co2 = (data["CO2_ppm"] - data["CO2_ppm"].min()) / (data["CO2_ppm"].max() - data["CO2_ppm"].min()) * 0.6 + 0.3
scale_ice = (data["sea_ice_mkm2"] - data["sea_ice_mkm2"].min()) / (data["sea_ice_mkm2"].max() - data["sea_ice_mkm2"].min()) * 0.6 + 0.3

plotter = pv.Plotter(window_size=[1100, 700])
plotter.set_background("white")

    3 · Add 3D spheres and render
    reds  = plt.cm.Reds(np.linspace(0.4, 1.0, len(data)))[:, :3]
blues = plt.cm.Blues_r(np.linspace(0.3, 1.0, len(data)))[:, :3]

for i in range(len(data)):
    sphere = pv.Sphere(radius=scale_co2[i], center=(x[i], y_top[i], 0))
    plotter.add_mesh(sphere, color=tuple(reds[i]),
                     smooth_shading=True, opacity=0.35,
                     specular=0.6, ambient=0.25)

for i in range(len(data)):
    sphere = pv.Sphere(radius=scale_ice[i], center=(x[i], y_bottom[i], 0))
    plotter.add_mesh(sphere, color=tuple(blues[i]),
                     smooth_shading=True, opacity=0.4,
                     specular=0.6, ambient=0.25)

plotter.camera_position = [(8, 8, 5), (0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)]
plotter.show(screenshot="co2_seaice_3d_pyvista.png")

    Climate & Art
    Where climate science meets Adobe Illustrator visual storytelling.
  

  

    
      
      
        an inconvenient data
        An Inconvenient Truth was one of the first climate films I watched, and one of the most striking. Released in 2006, it turned Al Gore's slideshow into a cultural moment, bringing the science of global warming to a mainstream audience long before climate communication became a field of its own.
        The poster stayed with me. So I made my own version: the factory chimneys from the original poster replaced by racks of an HPC cluster. The smoke rising from them is no longer industrial pollution, but Ed Hawkins' Climate Stripes: blue fading into red, decade by decade. Same image, different source. Same story.
      
    

    
      
      
        año 2021 en la tierra
        One Day on Earth is a documentary project that captures a single day on the planet through thousands of simultaneous recordings. I took that idea and made it my own: a film reel, but instead of one day, the entire 2021, told through images of climate events.
        The title is in Spanish — Año 2021 en la Tierra, Year 2021 on Earth. A polar bear stranded on shrinking ice, wildfires tearing through landscapes across three continents, smoke where there used to be sky. Each frame a document. Each year that year.

    Seasonal Forecasting & Climate Services at AEMET
    
      🌦️ Tragsatec – AEMET
      📍 Spain · Hybrid
      📅 Sep 2024 – Present
    
  

  

    

      Since September 2024 I have been working as a Climate Scientist for Tragsatec, providing climate services to Spain's national meteorological agency (AEMET). The work sits at the intersection of statistical climatology, geospatial analysis, and data communication — translating complex seasonal forecast products into accessible, interactive tools for decision-makers and the public.

      Seasonal forecasting operates on timescales of one to six months ahead, using statistical post-processing techniques to calibrate the output of global climate models against observed data. The challenge is not only scientific — it is also communicative. A seasonal forecast is only useful if the people who need it can understand and act on it.

      
        This project is the one where I have pushed furthest into data communication and interactive visualisation. Building dashboards in Plotly, Dash and Shiny, writing D3.js components, and working with Datawrapper for public-facing outputs has changed how I think about the relationship between climate data and the people who need it.
      

      What I do
      
        Seasonal forecasting and statistical post-processing of global climate model output
        Geospatial analysis of climate variables across the Spanish territory
        Interactive dashboard development with Plotly, Dash and Shiny
        Data visualisation for public and institutional audiences using D3.js and Datawrapper
        Workflow automation and batch processing in HPC environments using Bash

    Paleoclimate · Research
    Palaeoclimate Research at University College London
    
      🏛️ University College London
      📍 London, United Kingdom
      📅 2018
    
  

  

    

      After completing my PhD, I joined one of the world's leading research universities to work at the intersection of palaeoclimate science and computational modelling. UCL's Department of Geography is home to some of the most respected palaeoclimate researchers in Europe, and joining that environment — even for a year — was a formative experience.

      The project focused on stalagmites as climate proxies. Stalagmites grow inside caves over thousands of years, and their chemical composition records past changes in temperature, rainfall, and atmospheric circulation. By simulating how stalagmites grow, we can reconstruct what the climate looked like long before instrumental records began.

      
        Working at UCL meant attending interdisciplinary project meetings in London and Reading, collaborating with geologists, isotope chemists and climate modellers, and learning to communicate across very different scientific cultures. It also pushed my Python skills in a new direction — building physical simulations from scratch rather than postprocessing model output.
      

      What I did
      
        Developed a Python model to simulate stalagmite growth behaviour from first principles
        Built a comprehensive database of speleothem proxy climate records
        Wrote scientific reports and contributed to project documentation
        Attended research meetings in London and Reading with interdisciplinary teams

    PhD · Atmospheric Physics
    Precipitation Recycling and Land–Atmosphere Interactions over Europe
    
      🎓 Universidade de Santiago de Compostela
      📍 Santiago de Compostela + Lisboa
      📅 Oct 2014 – Dec 2017
      🏅 Merit · European Doctorate Mention
    
  

  

    

      This thesis set out to improve understanding of the role of land–atmosphere interactions in the climate system, with particular focus on evapotranspiration fluxes and precipitation processes over selected regions of the European continent. The primary tool was the WRF-ARW regional meteorological model, coupled with the hydrological model LeafHydro.

      The results demonstrated the importance of precipitation recycling processes — how moisture evaporated from the land surface feeds back into rainfall — and quantified the impact of using a fully coupled hydrology–atmosphere modelling system on the simulated climate of Europe. These findings have implications for how we model water availability under future climate scenarios.

      
        The thesis received the European Doctorate Mention, which required a six-month visiting stay at a foreign institution and the defence of part of the work in a language other than Spanish. I completed that stay at the University of Lisbon (Feb–Jul 2017), where I ran WRF–LeafHydro simulations and contributed to joint analyses.
      

      What I did
      
        Ran and postprocessed regional climate simulations with WRF-ARW coupled to the LeafHydro hydrological model
        Analysed evapotranspiration and precipitation recycling rates across Europe using model output and observational datasets
        Completed a five-month visiting research stay at the University of Lisbon
        Wrote the PhD dissertation, scientific reports and conference posters
        Supervised undergraduate students in their end-of-degree projects

    EU Project · Coastal Climate Adaptation
    MarRISK — Coastal Risk Assessment for Northwest Iberia
    
      🌊 MeteoGalicia
      📍 Santiago de Compostela, Spain
      📅 2018 – 2021
      💶 Budget: €3.5M
    
  

  

    

      MarRISK was a European Interreg POCTEP project focused on climate change adaptation for the coastlines of Galicia and Northern Portugal. The goal was to evaluate the most significant coastal risks under future climate scenarios — flooding, extreme events, toxic algal blooms, coastal erosion — and improve the resilience of traditional economic sectors and emerging industries such as marine renewable energy.

      I joined the project as a climate scientist at MeteoGalicia, the regional meteorological service of Galicia, where I worked on the oceanographic and climate components of the project. My work involved processing large volumes of model output and observational buoy data to characterise the current and projected coastal climate of the region.

      
        MarRISK brought together researchers, public authorities and stakeholders from both sides of the Spanish-Portuguese border. That cross-border collaboration — coordinating with partners in Vigo, Porto and Lisbon, communicating results to non-scientific audiences — was as valuable as the technical work itself.
      

      What I did
      
        Processed outputs from oceanographic models and observational buoy networks along the Galician and Northern Portuguese coast
        Conducted regional climate analysis to characterise present and projected future conditions
        Prepared scientific and technical reports on coastal climate risks
        Contributed to stakeholder communication and project dissemination materials

        PythonOceanographic modellingBuoy data processing
